09d01588fa:
This capstone builds the Structured Data Extraction scenario from the official guide. Unstructured documents go in. Validated records come out, with edge cases handled, for a downstream system that won't accept a malformed or wrong payload.

Chapters 12 and 13 explained the mechanisms one at a time: tool use with JSON schemas, tool_choice, nullable fields, validation and retry, detected_pattern, the Message Batches API.

Here they meet in one codebase that runs end to end on 60 synthetic documents, with ground truth. Every design decision produces a number you can check.
52861b2791:
The documents are the ones a telecom shared-services team actually sees:

  • supplier invoices for fibre, small-cell and tower work;
  • expense receipts from field technicians;
  • telecom service contracts (fibre broadband, mobile fleet, SIP trunking, MPLS, and two services that fit none of those).

Some invoices have no PO number, or say "see attached" where the PO should be. Some totals don't add up. Some are in EUR with 1.234,56 formatting, GBP with day-first dates, CAD, and one INR. A receipt says "Paid: Card" and nothing else. A contract states its term as "3 years".
9ceb31d61e:
The whole pipeline runs offline. A rule-based MockClient stands in for the Messages API, and a FakeBatchBackend for the Message Batches API. Both use the same method names as the real SDK, so switching to the real API takes one environment variable.

The mock makes realistic mistakes on purpose. Validation catches some of them. Only ground truth reveals the others. A pipeline that's only ever shown correct output teaches you nothing about where it breaks.
d5b1e87738:
As in Capstone A, start by sorting requirements by kind. The exam keeps testing whether you know which mechanism gives which guarantee.

  • Tool use guarantees the shape of the output.
  • Code guarantees invariants about the values.
  • The prompt and examples make good values likely.
  • Measurement against ground truth tells you how likely, per segment.
bba5d11a21:
Two decisions shape the rest of the build.

First, there's one Pydantic model per document type, and the tool schemas are generated from those models. The same classes validate the output. So the schema the model sees and the schema the validator enforces can't drift apart.

In Spring terms, this is generating the OpenAPI contract and the request DTOs from one source, instead of maintaining both by hand.
3fbbf72763:
Second, the real-time path and the batch path send identical requests. batch.py calls the same request_params() that realtime.py uses, and the same validate() on the results. Only the transport and the retry rhythm differ.

That's what lets you prove a prompt on the real-time path with a few documents, then move the bulk to batch without re-testing a different system.
20e2bcc046:
Read the diagram left to right.

Extraction is a single Messages API call. When the document type is known (the mailroom already sorted it), one tool is offered and tool_choice is forced to it. When it isn't, all three tools are offered with tool_choice: {"type": "any"}.

Validation runs the Pydantic model, then the semantic checks. A retryable failure goes back to the model in the same conversation, as an error tool result. Two cases go to the human queue as needs_review: anything still failing after two retries, and anything failing because the information isn't in the document.

Accepted records then face a second gate. Each field's confidence must clear that field's calibrated threshold. If not, the record goes to review with just the doubtful fields highlighted.
cc8c7981e4: The batch box sits beside extraction, not after it. It's a different way of running the same request, chosen per workload. The overnight backlog of 40,000 supplier invoices goes to batch. A contract that a sales engineer uploads during a customer call goes real-time.
e113fb5504:
You can't evaluate extraction without labels. And you can't get honest labels from the same model you're evaluating.

So the generator produces the document text and the correct record from the same random draw. It decides the invoice number, dates, line items and currency first, then renders them in one of several layouts. The label is exact by construction.

It's seeded, so the corpus is identical on every machine and the tests can assert specific outcomes.
3ac29b4e37: Each difficulty is placed deliberately, and recorded in the label as an expected anomaly pattern:
8168308a6b:
The split deserves a word of its own.

The first version alternated documents within each type. That put every one-line GBP receipt (the hardest dates) into one half. Calibration never saw those cases, and approved thresholds that let wrong dates through on the other half.

The fix was to stratify by (type, layout). A test now asserts that both halves contain all seven strata.

It's the same trap task 5.5 warns about with aggregate metrics. A sample that's random overall can still be empty for the segment that matters.
9041d44f3c: Four schema rules from task 4.3 carry the design. Each one removes a specific pressure on the model to produce a wrong value.
b58717667a: Required but nullable. Every field the source might lack is listed in required and typed X | null. The model must emit the key and make an explicit choice. A non-nullable po_number: str forces it to put something there, and you get "see attached" or an invented PO. An optional (not required) field lets it silently drop the key. Then you can't tell "absent in the document" from "forgot".
17b2aee298: "other" plus detail. A closed enum with no escape hatch forces a near miss: SD-WAN gets recorded as mpls. With "other" and service_type_detail, the record stays honest. The detail field tells you which enum value to add next quarter.
855f5d62ff: "unclear". This is different from "other". "Paid: Card" isn't an unlisted payment method. It's a document that doesn't say whether it was credit or debit. "unclear" records that, and it routes differently.
67f2f5a894: Self-checks in the schema. stated_total (copied) and calculated_total (computed by the model) sit side by side. There's field_confidence per field, and anomalies[].detected_pattern as an enum. The only job of these fields is to make the output checkable.
bed4c1b8c6:
Optional[X] = Field(...) is how Pydantic spells required-but-nullable. The ellipsis makes the key required, and Optional allows null.

The generated JSON Schema contains anyOf: [{type: string}, {type: null}], with the field name in required. A test asserts exactly that, because a well-meaning = None default breaks it easily.
4519f8bafb: Field descriptions do real work. "The party that issued the invoice, not a remit-to/factoring company" is a normalisation rule, placed at the point of use. Tool and field descriptions are part of the prompt the model reads. Task 2.1 makes the same point for tool selection.
029d05ab4b:
Inlining the $defs is a defensive choice, not a requirement. A flat schema is easier to read in logs and to diff between prompt versions. It also avoids depending on how any consumer resolves references.

The in_props flag strips Pydantic's cosmetic titles while keeping any property that happens to be named title.
73792ba6e6:
There are three tools, one per document type: record_invoice, record_receipt and record_service_contract.

A single generic extract_document tool with a union schema would be smaller to write and worse to use. The model would have to pick a branch inside a large schema. And the descriptions couldn't say what each type is not.

Separate tools turn classification into tool selection, which is what tool descriptions are built for.
f6454c747e:
With any, the run over all 60 documents classifies each one correctly by tool choice alone. A test checks it.

Notice what any doesn't guarantee: that the right tool is chosen. A half-invoice, half-receipt scan will still produce a schema-valid record of one type. If misclassification is costly, classify first (a cheap call, or rules), then extract with a forced tool.
2231de9e2f:
The system prompt carries the normalisation rules and four few-shot examples. The rules are numbered, so validation feedback and reviewers can refer to them.

The examples cover exactly the cases where the rules alone left the mock (and, in practice, models) inconsistent:

  • a referenced but absent PO;
  • totals that don't add up;
  • a GBP slash date with an unresolvable payment method;
  • a service outside the enum, with a term in years.

Task 4.2 says few-shot examples are most useful for ambiguous cases, and that's where these sit. There's no example of a clean USD invoice, because the model doesn't need one.
50d59d231a: Each example shows the wrong answer as well as the right one. "Wrong: changing stated_total to 345.60, or dropping a line so the numbers agree" names the exact shortcut a model takes when asked to produce a consistent record from an inconsistent document.
4ecc7f07b7:
Forced tool use removes JSON syntax errors. It doesn't stop an amount arriving as the string "1.234,56", a currency of "INR" outside the enum, or a calculated_total that forgot the tax.

The validator has two layers, and it classifies every problem by whether a retry can fix it:
d266649f02:
Three details are worth copying.

  • The validator recomputes the arithmetic itself rather than trusting the model's calculated_total. The model's number is a self-check, and the validator checks the self-check.
  • The mismatch rule doesn't reject a document whose printed total is wrong. It rejects a record that hides the problem. Both totals stay, and the anomaly makes the inconsistency visible downstream.
  • Every message says what to do next ("Recompute it; do not change stated_total"), because the message goes back to the model as feedback.
88666e45ae: A null is never a validation error by itself. invoice_date: null on an invoice that prints no date is the correct answer, and a test asserts that such a record validates clean. Require a value there and the validator becomes a machine for producing fabrications.
04e719a11d:
The loop sends the request and validates the tool input. On a retryable failure, it appends two turns to the same conversation:

  • the assistant's tool_use block, exactly as received;
  • a user turn with a tool_result for that tool_use_id, marked is_error: true, whose content is the validator's feedback.

The model then sees what it produced, and precisely what was wrong with it. tool_choice stays forced on the retry, so the answer is again a record and not an apology.
999eb2e9fc:
What goes into the retry matters as much as the decision to retry. The feedback lists only retryable issues, one line per field. It ends with "Values that are not in the document must stay null; do not invent them."

That last line is there for a reason. The most common bad reaction to "po_number is a reference, not a PO number" is to produce a plausible-looking PO number.

In the default run, inv_000 and inv_016 come back on the second attempt with po_number: null and a missing_po_number anomaly. That's the right outcome.
ff37dd6bdb:
The loop has three exits, and only one of them counts attempts.

  • A clean record returns at once.
  • A record whose only issues are absent_source goes to needs_review after one call. Two more calls on an illegible scan buy nothing (task 4.4: retries are ineffective when the information is absent from the source).
  • Anything else gets at most two retries.

The cap exists because some failures are systematic. If a prompt rule is unclear, the third attempt makes the same mistake as the first. A human seeing it is the fastest way to find the rule that needs fixing.
d5ac023aba:
If you've built Spring Retry policies, the structure is familiar. Classify exceptions into retryable and non-retryable, bound the attempts, and send the rest to a dead-letter queue.

The difference is that the "exception message" is input to the next attempt. A retry that resends the same request without the error is like retrying a 400 Bad Request unchanged.
532d62f3a9:
MockClient implements client.messages.create(...) and client.messages.batches.{create, retrieve, results} with the same keyword arguments as the SDK. It returns objects with the same attributes (content[i].type, .id, .name, .input, usage.input_tokens, processing_status, result.type).

Underneath, it's a set of regular-expression parsers for the seven layouts. It honours tool_choice. Forced means that tool. any means it classifies the document by its cues. auto returns a sentence of prose, which is how the test for "never use auto" works.
51ac08f3d8: A mock that's always right would make every test pass and teach nothing. This one has two families of mistakes, chosen to match what real extraction systems get wrong:
549620c3cd:
The second family is the important one.

A validator can't tell that "Apex Receivables Finance" is the remit-to company rather than the vendor. The record is internally consistent. Only labelled data reveals the error. And only calibration on labelled data stops a 0.90 self-reported confidence from waving it through.

The mock gives honest low confidence on the ambiguous dates, and overconfident high confidence on the vendor and card cases. Expect the same pattern from real models. They're often well calibrated on what they know is ambiguous, and poorly calibrated on what they don't realise is a trap.
ca456baf39:
_is_retry() looks for a tool_result block with is_error: true in the last user turn. So the mock only improves when the pipeline sends the feedback the way task 4.4 describes. A loop that resends the original request unchanged gets the same broken record back, exactly as it would from a real model.

stubborn_markers makes a document unfixable, so the tests can prove the cap of two retries.
91ef8cf1ad:
The backlog path uses the Message Batches API. There's one request per document, with custom_id set to the document id and the params built by the same request_params().

The batch is created and polled until processing_status is "ended". Only then are results read. Results are joined by custom_id. The fake backend returns them in reverse order on purpose, so any code that relies on position fails its tests.
2076a86aef:
A batch request is one Messages API call. It can't run a tool loop: there's nobody inside the batch to execute a tool and send the result back (task 4.5).

That doesn't rule out the retry, because extraction needs no tool execution. The "tool" is only a schema. The retry simply moves to the next batch round, carrying the assistant turn and the is_error result in its messages.

The cost is latency, since each round can take up to 24 hours. That's why the round count is capped, and why the SLA arithmetic below has a safety margin.
b445abbf48:
Batch requests are billed at about half the standard rate (at the time of writing; check the pricing page). The code takes prices as parameters and prints a relative figure, so no price is baked into the repository. On the same tokens, batch is exactly 50% of real-time.

The resubmission rounds add only the failed documents' tokens. Resubmitting the whole batch because 16 items failed would cost 60 documents' worth again.
d4339d6445:
The reasoning is worst case, not typical case. A document that arrives one minute after a batch is cut waits a full interval for the next one. And that batch is allowed 24 hours.

With a 30-hour SLA and a 2-hour margin, the interval is 4 hours, which matches the example in the exam guide. At 24 or 26 hours, the function returns None. Batch can't guarantee the SLA, even if it usually finishes in an hour. Those documents belong on the real-time path.

Note that a second batch round for failures eats into the same margin. If your failure rate is high, either raise the margin or send round-2 items through the real-time path.
ea91d3205e:
Every record carries field_confidence. But a number the model reports about itself is a ranking signal, not a probability. A 0.92 on "Paid: Card" means nothing until you know how often 0.92 was right for that field.

Task 5.5 says to calibrate thresholds with labelled validation data, and to keep sampling the high-confidence output. route.py does both.
206c97082f:
On the default run, the calibrated threshold is 0.97 for invoice.vendor_name and 0.95 for receipt.payment_method. Both sit above the overconfident wrong answers (0.90 and 0.92), because the validation split contains examples of each.

Some fields get a lower bar. Where the model reports 0.88 for an inference that's always right, such as contract.service_type mapped to "other", the threshold is 0.88. One global threshold can't express both. The result on the 28-document test split:
98d44a8873:
The calibrated policy accepts more documents and makes fewer mistakes. It's strict where the model is overconfident, and lenient where its low numbers are just modesty.

The audit sample is stratified by document type, with at least one per type. A 2% uniform random sample of a mix dominated by invoices could easily contain no contracts for weeks. Stratifying guarantees that drift in a small segment shows up in the audit.
b4e0a0a180:
min_support guards against small samples. With three or four validation examples per field, a single lucky high-confidence answer could set a threshold.

Raising min_support pushes more fields to NEVER (always reviewed) until you have enough labels. That's the right direction to fail in. When you can't measure a field, a human checks it.
49c63abd95:
report.py runs the real-time path on all 60 documents and compares every scored field with ground truth. It reports:

  • field accuracy, and document accuracy (every scored field correct), per type;
  • accuracy per field;
  • a precision and recall table per detected_pattern;
  • the routing comparison above.

Thresholds are fitted on the validation split, and routing is judged on the test split. So the routing numbers aren't measured on the data that set them.
a2cd213780:
Read it top down.

98.2% field accuracy would pass most dashboards. Document accuracy, which decides whether a person touches the record, is 85%. And receipts, a third of the volume, are at 66.7%: one in three receipts has a wrong field.

Two fields explain it: transaction_date (one-line GBP receipts read month-first) and payment_method ("Paid: Card"). Each has a specific fix. The first is a prompt or parsing fix for one layout. The second is the "unclear" rule, which the prompt already states and the mock ignores.

Neither shows up in the aggregate.
8c54fe68a1:
The pattern table does the same job for the anomaly flags. Four patterns have precision 1.0. ambiguous_date has 0.55: it also fires on US month-first dates, where the currency settles the order.

Without detected_pattern, you'd only know that "about a fifth of the flags are wrong". The tempting response is to stop trusting flags altogether. With it, you know which rule to tighten, and you can leave the other four alone. That's the purpose task 4.4 gives the field.
ac7bb2af6b:
Run the real-time path on a stratified sample of 10 to 20 documents first, and read the failures. Task 4.5 recommends refining the prompt on a sample before processing the full set. A prompt error found after a 40,000-document batch costs the whole batch.

The mock's results won't match a real model's. Expect different weak fields. Treat the report as the tool for finding them, not as a prediction.
aef8e636f6:
The pipeline runs offline on 60 synthetic documents: 24 invoices in three layouts, 18 receipts, 18 telecom service contracts. The hard cases are seeded:

  • missing PO numbers and dates;
  • "see attached" in the PO field;
  • totals that don't add up;
  • euro amounts written 1.234,56;
  • dd/mm British dates;
  • an Indian rupee invoice;
  • "Paid: Card";
  • service types outside the enum.

A rule-based mock client plays the model, and it makes the mistakes a model plausibly makes. Everything below was captured from real runs of realtime.py, batch.py and report.py.
2f5cd4fe28:
Fourteen of 60 documents failed validation on the first attempt and were fixed by one retry. (The number is the attempt count, so each succeeded on the second.) The causes are the ones the schema and validator were built for: amounts sent as strings, a currency outside the enum, other without detail, a calculated total that forgot tax, and "see attached" stored as a PO number. All 60 end accepted.

Two things in that result deserve a careful read.

The two invoices whose PO field says "see attached" end with po_number: null, not a fabricated value. The information is absent from the document, and the nullable field is the honest answer.

And "60 accepted" is a statement about validation, not about correctness. A record can pass every check and still be wrong. That's exactly what the report below measures.
2dc6b2f080:
The first batch submits 60 requests, each with a custom_id equal to the document id. It polls until the batch has ended. Then it joins results by custom_id, never by position, because result order isn't guaranteed.

Sixteen fail: fourteen invalid (the same validation failures as before), one errored (ctr_003) and one expired (rcp_010). Only those 16 go into the second batch, with the validation errors attached for the invalid ones. The second batch returns all 16.

Resubmitting the full 60 would have paid again for 44 good results. The cost line shows the 50 percent price difference: 0.2054 versus 0.1027 in relative units, for the same tokens.
b617f40a43:
The SLA lines are the part people skip.

If the business needs results within a deadline, the submission interval is that deadline minus the batch processing window, minus the time to resubmit failures. With a 30-hour SLA, the helper says submit every 4 hours. With 48 hours, every 22. With 24 or 26 hours it says None: no schedule can promise it. The batch window alone is up to 24 hours, and a retry round needs room.

Batch is for latency-tolerant work. An SLA close to the batch window isn't latency-tolerant. The first official sample question in the exam turns on this reasoning.
e9c1430b4a:
Field accuracy of 98.2 percent sounds like a pipeline you can switch on. Document accuracy, the share of documents with every field right, is 85 percent. For receipts, it's 66.7 percent.

Three fields explain most of it:

  • receipt.transaction_date at 72.2 percent (British dd/mm dates read month-first on one-line receipts);
  • receipt.payment_method at 88.9 percent ("Paid: Card" mapped to credit_card);
  • invoice.vendor_name at 87.5 percent (a remit-to factoring line taken as the vendor).

The report flags receipts as weak. This is the aggregate-masks-segment failure of Chapter 16, reproduced with real numbers from a fixture.

The thresholds in the right-hand column are calibrated per field on the validation split. A field the model gets wrong while sounding confident gets a high threshold, so fewer of its values are auto-accepted.
659e328a4c:
Each anomaly the model flags carries a detected_pattern, so false positives can be analysed by pattern (task 4.4). ambiguous_date has precision 0.55: it flagged 5 dates that weren't ambiguous. The other four patterns are perfect on this fixture.

The action the exam describes is targeted. Tighten or temporarily disable the noisy pattern, and leave the others. A high false-positive category erodes trust in the whole flag stream.
e2d4b4d5ef:
The comparison is the point of calibration. Per-field thresholds auto-accept 19 of 28 test documents, and all 19 are fully correct.

A single global cut-off of 0.90 accepts fewer (11) and is less accurate (90.9 percent). The model is overconfident on two fields. So a global threshold lets wrong values through, while holding back right ones from fields that were reliable. Calibrated routing is both safer and cheaper in reviewer time.

The audit sample is the continuing control: 2 percent of the auto-accepted output, stratified by type, drawn at random, reviewed by a person.

These are 28 documents, which is a small test set. Treat the pattern as the lesson, and the numbers as fixture output.
6ca6c6b0c6:
The retry tests make one detail checkable that's easy to get wrong in live code. The corrective message must be a tool_result with is_error: true, whose tool_use_id matches the preceding tool_use.

The Messages API rejects a conversation where a tool_use isn't followed by its result. So a retry that appends plain user text instead fails with a 400 on the live API. (The mock enforces the same pairing.)

The test for "an absent date triggers no retry" is the executable version of "retries are ineffective when the information is absent from the source".
80087a0fb0:
Four numbers keep this pipeline honest.

  • First-pass validity: the share of documents that pass without a retry (46 of 60 in the fixture). It falls when a supplier changes a layout or a model version changes behaviour, and it's the earliest signal.
  • Retry success rate and needs_review rate, per document type. They show whether the corrective feedback works, and how much human work the pipeline creates.
  • Audit accuracy, from the random sample of auto-accepted output, with a confidence interval (Chapter 16). It's the only measurement of the error rate that reached production.
  • Cost per accepted record, split by real-time and batch. It shows whether the batch share is as high as it should be.

Pin the model version in configuration, and rerun calibration when it changes. Thresholds fitted on one model don't transfer to another.
696fdb77f9:
Move documents between lanes deliberately. Anything with a person waiting (an invoice being keyed into a payment run today) goes real-time. Anything that can wait a day (the backlog, month-end reconciliation, a re-extraction after a schema change) goes through batch.

The validator and the schemas are shared. So the same record shape comes out of both lanes, and the router treats them identically.
cdd26497a7:
The Pydantic models become Java records with Bean Validation. The tool schema can be generated from them, with a JSON Schema generator, or by hand for the small number of types.

The validator is an ordinary service that returns a list of issues, each with a kind. The retry loop is a bounded loop around the client call.
8f309f03dc: Fix the ambiguous_date precision of 0.55 without disabling the pattern. What would you change in the prompt or the validator? How do you show that precision improved without losing recall?
6889d6e791: Replace the stratified audit with one weighted toward the types with the lowest document accuracy. What bias does that introduce into the overall error estimate, and how do you correct it?
9569b72463: Run the real-time path against the live API for ten documents (CAPD_LIVE=1). Compare its first-pass validity with the mock's 46 of 60, and explain the difference.
bb5d3c73f6: Every row is a pytest test that runs offline. Together, they're the capstone's definition of done, and a revision sheet for the five task statements.
6d3b676ec7: Each drill changes one thing and predicts what the tests and the report should show. Run them after the suite is green. They turn exam phrases into behaviour you've actually seen.
11f7aed3e9: Separate the two symptoms. The wrong vendor on factored invoices is a semantic error the schema can't catch: both names are strings. The non-existent PO numbers are fabrications. The model filled a field that should have been null.
cd44a7e132: Fabricated POs point at the schema and prompt. Check whether po_number is non-nullable or not required. Make it required-but-nullable. Add the rule that references like "see attached" aren't values, and add the few-shot example. Add a validator check (no digits means it's a reference) that returns a specific is_error message. Don't add "please don't invent PO numbers" on its own; that's the weakest option.
7b88e67541: Wrong vendor points at calibration. The model reports 0.9 on the factored invoices, so a global 0.9 threshold lets them through. Measure accuracy by field on labelled data that includes factored invoices. Calibrate the vendor_name threshold per field. Add the vendor-versus-remit-to rule to the field description and the prompt.
8a96cf8257: Do not trust the 97%. Break it down by document type and field. Here, contracts and clean invoices dominate the aggregate. The factored-invoice segment is small, and wrong.
1d7c032566: Keep checking the auto path. Add a stratified audit of auto-accepted records. Then a new pattern, such as a new factoring company layout, is caught before finance finds it.
1c7164a9ec:
The distractors you'd reject:

  • "switch to a larger model": it doesn't address fabrication pressure or calibration;
  • "lower the threshold to 0.8": the wrong direction;
  • "add retries": the records pass validation, so nothing triggers a retry;
  • "use tool_choice any": the type is already known.
d845946562: Create the venv and install pydantic pytest. Run python generate_docs.py, then pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider tests. Done when 40 tests pass with no network access.
28a09861ba: Run python realtime.py and open runs/realtime.jsonl. Pick inv_019 and inv_016 and read their trail. Done when you can say, for each, which validator rule fired, what the feedback said, and what changed on attempt 2.
aa485377d1: Run python report.py. Done when you can name the weak type, the two fields responsible, and the one noisy detected_pattern. You should also be able to explain why the calibrated policy accepts more documents than the global 0.90 policy while being more accurate.
bb5eb15e34: Run python batch.py. Then set polls_until_done = 5 on the fake backend and inject three more expired results. Done when round 2 contains exactly the failed custom_ids, and you can explain how a third round would affect a 30-hour SLA.
fcd4604a53: Extension: add a fourth type, credit_note, with negative amounts and a reference to an original invoice number. Add the Pydantic model, a tool, two few-shot cases, and a validator rule (amounts must be negative; the original invoice number must not equal its own number). Add five generated documents and labels. Done when all tests pass and the report shows the new type.
